feedback: If the piece is named a 'smaller third', re-extend the cut lines across the whole bar and count all 12 equal parts — the whole has been re-ruled, so the new unit is a twelfth.
If the learner cannot say where 12 comes from, point to the 3 original parts and the 4 cuts in each: 3 × 4 = 12.
Confirm by reassembling: 4 twelfths placed side by side exactly cover the original third, so 1/12 × 4 = 1/3.
A number line gives the same result: the 0–1/3 segment splitting into 4 sub-segments of 1/12 mirrors the bar being re-ruled into twelfths.
activities.intendedInsight: Sharing one-third among 4 cuts the whole into twelfths because the second cut (into 4) multiplies the first partition (into 3): 3 × 4 = 12. The answer is smaller than 1/3, and the denominator grows because the whole is re-partitioned more finely — this is the picture, not a memorised rule.
learnerActions: Start with a whole bar that has one-third shaded.
Apply a '÷4' cut to the shaded third so it splits into 4 equal parts.

Re-rule the WHOLE bar the same way: if your cuts run along the bar (crossing the third-lines), extend them across the whole bar; if they run across the bar like the third-lines, cut each of the other two thirds into 4 equal parts too. Count: the whole is now ruled into 12 equal parts.
Read off one little shaded piece and name it: it is one-twelfth, not a smaller third.
Say out loud where 12 comes from: 3 original parts, each cut into 4, gives 3 × 4 = 12.
Gather 4 of the twelfths back together to remake the original third, confirming 1/12 × 4 = 1/3.
Optionally repeat on a number line: split the 0–1/3 segment into 4 equal sub-segments and see each is 1/12 of the whole 0–1 line.
activities.title: Share a third four ways on a bar

feedback: If a learner inverts 1/3 ÷ 4 to 1/3 × 4 = 4/3, ask them to describe in words what is being shared and into how many parts — sharing a third cannot give each person more than a third, let alone more than a whole.
If stories are mismatched, re-read each for the action word: 'share among' signals splitting (smaller); 'how many fit' signals counting (bigger).
Re-use one bar for both questions so the two actions sit on the same picture.
activities.intendedInsight: Dividing a unit fraction by a whole number (sharing) and dividing a whole number by a unit fraction (measuring how many fit) are different meanings with opposite size effects. Naming which is happening HERE prevents over-generalising 'dividing by fractions makes it bigger'.
learnerActions: Work two questions side by side on bars: 'share 1/3 among 4' (1/3 ÷ 4) and 'how many fifths fit in 4?' (4 ÷ 1/5).
For each, say aloud which action is happening: splitting one piece into more pieces, or counting how many pieces fit.
Predict before computing whether each answer is bigger or smaller than the starting number, and why.
Match short stories ('share this third between four of you' / 'how many 1/5 cups fill 4 cups?') to the correct ÷ expression.

State the rule-of-thumb in meaning terms for these cases: sharing among 2 or more makes each part smaller than the amount shared; counting how many unit fractions (smaller than 1) fit into a whole number gives an answer larger than that whole number.
activities.title: Share vs. how-many-fit: the sibling contrast

feedback: If a learner writes 1/6 ÷ 3 = 1/9, show that sharing multiplies the parts (6 parts each cut into 3 = 18), it does not add 3 to the bottom.
If the story describes 'how many fit' instead of sharing, rewrite it so one amount is split among a number of people.
Always close by reassembling the m pieces to recover the original fraction as a check.
activities.intendedInsight: The partition method generalises: for any unit fraction 1/n ÷ m, splitting each of the n parts into m re-rules the whole into n × m parts, so each piece is 1/(n×m). Whenever the fraction is shared among 2 or more (m ≥ 2) the piece is smaller than the original; sharing among 1 would leave it unchanged.
learnerActions: Take a new case such as 1/6 ÷ 3 and write a short sharing story for it (e.g. 'share one-sixth of a pizza between 3').

Draw a bar with one-sixth shaded and split that sixth into 3 equal parts, then re-rule the whole the same way (extend cuts that cross the sixth-lines across the bar, or cut every other sixth into 3 too).
Count the total equal parts the whole is now cut into (6 × 3 = 18) and name one piece (1/18).
Verify with the inverse: 1/18 × 3 = 1/6.
Explain how you found the bottom number, referring to the two cuts, not an added-on rule.
activities.title: Build and solve your own sharing story

feedback: 4/3 comes from multiplying instead of dividing (1/3 × 4 = 4/3), possibly from over-applying 'dividing with fractions makes bigger'; but sharing a third among 4 must give something smaller than a third, so 4/3 cannot be right.
1/7 treats ÷4 as '+4 on the bottom'; sharing multiplies the parts (3 × 4 = 12), so re-cut and count the 12 pieces.
The answer 1/12 only counts as secure when the learner can name why the pieces are twelfths — if they call them 'thirds', rebuild the partition and count the 12 parts.
activities.intendedInsight: A secure answer is 1/12 WITH an explanation that the whole is cut more finely into twelfths; the characteristic errors are 4/3 (multiplying instead of dividing, possibly from over-applying 'dividing with fractions makes bigger') and 1/7 (adding the whole number to the denominator).
learnerActions: Answer: 1/3 ÷ 4 = ? choosing from 1/12, 4/3, 1/7.
For the chosen answer, state in one sentence whether it is bigger or smaller than 1/3 and why.
On a blank bar, draw the split of a shaded third into quarters and re-rule the whole bar the same way (extend cuts that cross the third-lines, or cut each third into 4) to show the twelfths.
Answer the second-tier probe: 'Point to one small piece — how do you know it is a twelfth and not a smaller third?'
activities.title: Check understanding with targeted distractors

feedback: If the learner cannot name the piece, invite them to describe or sketch the cuts — the naming follows from counting all equal parts of the whole.
Steer talk back to 'is it bigger or smaller than a third, and why' to keep the sharing meaning central.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating the sharing structure and the size comparison in words reinforces the partition meaning and can surface rule-following when a learner cannot name why the pieces are twelfths.
learnerActions: Take on a sharing-story role: 'split this third fairly between four of you'.
Discuss aloud whether each person's piece is bigger or smaller than a third, and justify it.
Explain how the pieces get their name (twelfths) by describing the cuts you would make.
activities.title: Talk-through sharing (optional discussion scaffold)
